{{Short description|Theorem about circles through lattice points}}
In the [[geometry of numbers]], Schinzel's theorem is the following statement:

{{math theorem|name=Schinzel's theorem|For any given [[positive integer]] <math>n</math>, there exists a [[circle]] in the [[Euclidean plane]] that passes through exactly <math>n</math> integer points.}}

It was originally proved by and named after [[Andrzej Schinzel]].{{r|schinzel|honsberger}}

== Proof ==

[[File:Schinzel Circle.png|thumb|upright=1.35|Circle through exactly four points given by Schinzel's construction]]
Schinzel proved this theorem by the following construction. If <math>n</math> is an even number, with <math>n=2k</math>, then the circle given by the following equation passes through exactly <math>n</math> points:{{r|schinzel|honsberger}}
<math display=block>\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 + y^2 =  \frac{1}{4} 5^{k-1}.</math>
This circle has radius <math>5^{(k-1)/2}/2</math>, and is centered at the point <math>(\tfrac12,0)</math>. For instance, the figure shows a circle with radius <math>\sqrt 5/2</math> through four integer points.

Multiplying both sides of Schinzel's equation by four produces an equivalent equation in integers,
<math display="block">\left(2x-1\right)^2 + (2y)^2 = 5^{k-1}.</math>
This writes <math>5^{k-1}</math> as a [[sum of two squares]], where the first is odd and the second is even. There are exactly <math>4k</math> ways to write <math>5^{k-1}</math> as a sum of two squares, and half are in the order (odd, even) by symmetry. For example, <math>5^1=(\pm 1)^2 + (\pm 2)^2</math>, so we have <math>2x-1=1</math> or <math>2x-1=-1</math>, and <math>2y=2</math> or <math>2y=-2</math>, which produces the four points pictured.

On the other hand, if <math>n</math> is odd, with <math>n=2k+1</math>, then the circle given by the following equation passes through exactly <math>n</math> points:{{r|schinzel|honsberger}}
<math display=block>\left(x-\frac{1}{3}\right)^2 + y^2 =  \frac{1}{9} 5^{2k}.</math>
This circle has radius <math>5^k/3</math>, and is centered at the point <math>(\tfrac13,0)</math>.

== Properties ==

The circles generated by Schinzel's construction are not the smallest possible circles passing through the given number of integer points,{{r|mathworld}} but they have the advantage that they are described by an explicit equation.{{r|honsberger}}
